overview: Hohokam is an archaeological label for related material traditions of ancestral Sonoran Desert communities, not the known name of a single ancient nation. The map’s 1492 to 1500 interval is misleading: the large settlement pattern described here had changed by about 1450. This card explains the earlier canal-building communities and their continuing descendants, rather than placing an unchanged state in that late outline.

periods.title: A map window after the major settlement changes
periods.summary: These imported years fall after the conventional archaeological endpoint around 1450. They do not date the communities’ foundation or the disappearance of their descendants.

sections.title: Water had to arrive at the right speed

items.text: Farmers built canals to bring river water to villages and fields. At S’edav Va’aki beside the Salt River, local bedrock helped direct water toward canal entrances. Choosing an intake location was an engineering decision tied to the landscape, before the long labour of digging even began.

A canal that slopes too steeply sends water racing against its banks; one too level lets silt settle and obstruct the flow. The builders had to find a workable gradient and keep maintaining it. Making water travel gently across a dry landscape was a lasting technical achievement.

Excavated pithouses leave postholes and hard, smooth floors, sometimes with caliche plaster. At Pueblo Grande, archaeologists also found pits where builders prepared caliche. Burned pieces of wall daub can preserve impressions of grass and wood, allowing vanished walls to leave surprisingly detailed clues.

Groups of houses faced shared courtyards. Archaeologists interpret these clusters as settings for cooperation among related households, including food preparation, weaving and child care. The layout is observable; the precise family relationships are an interpretation. A courtyard could be a workplace and a place to keep children nearby.

Manos and metates, handstones and larger grinding surfaces, reveal food preparation near homes. Plant residues can sometimes identify what was ground. Other finds, such as prepared clay, help locate pottery work. Cooking equipment and craft materials let researchers reconstruct activities on a household scale.

Cultivated foods included maize, beans and squash, while cotton supplied fibre. People also gathered cactus foods, mesquite pods and agave, and took fish and other animals. Irrigation did not make the surrounding desert irrelevant: families combined several sources of food and useful materials.

Pueblo Grande’s residents accumulated rubbish in mounds near their homes. Some surfaces appear to have been burned and covered with fresh soil, perhaps to control smells and pests. Ancient rubbish management also created a useful archive: yesterday’s discarded fragments can become today’s evidence for everyday life.

sections.title: Buildings large enough to bring people together

items.text: Oval depressions surrounded by earth banks are commonly called ballcourts. At S’edav Va’aki, the museum dates their wider importance to about 750 to 1200 and notes associations with exchange. Their exact activities remain uncertain; we cannot confidently supply teams, rules or a score for an ancient match.

The Great House at Casa Grande was built in the fourteenth century. Builders mixed local calcium-rich caliche with water and piled it into thick walls. Horizontal joins still mark successive courses left to dry before more material was added. The building preserves the rhythm of its construction.

The Great House also required wooden supports. The National Park Service describes timbers brought from forests as far as sixty miles away, with smaller saguaro ribs placed across supporting beams. A monument made from local earth still depended on planning, transport and materials from beyond the immediate settlement.

sections.title: A lizard waiting for its chemical bath

items.text: At Snaketown, excavators found a shell ornament with a horned-lizard design still protected by a resistant coating. It had not yet passed through the etching stage. This unfinished object helps explain how makers shielded parts of a surface while an acid removed the exposed shell around the design.

Shell specialist Chris Lange identifies fermented saguaro juice as a plausible weak acid for this process. Most dated etched-shell examples belong to about 950 to 1150. The objects show chemical craft knowledge, while the exact liquid used on an individual piece remains a proposed reconstruction.

sections.title: What can be read, and what continues

items.text: Casa Grande’s builders left no securely readable written language in the evidence presented by the National Park Service. Its written visitor history begins with Eusebio Kino in 1694, centuries later. There is no translated ancient sentence to show here; descendant communities’ oral histories and the archaeological record remain distinct sources of knowledge.

ending.text: Large settlements and canal networks changed during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries; this is not evidence that their people vanished. S’edav Va’aki’s museum describes movement into smaller villages after 1400 and identifies continuing Akimel O’odham descendants. The 1500 map endpoint supplies neither a conqueror nor a single cause for these changes.
